rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the late-elution penalty. The retention window will guide subsequent narrowing and slope or temperature adjustments.

The first method already reaches the maximum CRF, so shorten the gradient to seek an equally scoring, faster separation. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed isolates the effect of gradient steepness on the closest pair.

Shorten the gradient another grid step while holding temperature and endpoints fixed. The closest pair retained R = 2.46 at six minutes, suggesting a four-minute gradient may preserve full resolution and the maximum CRF.

The four-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF but leaves little resolution margin for the first pair. Raising temperature alone tests whether temperature selectivity can improve that pair while shortening retention.

Heating worsened the critical pair, so test the lowest temperature to favor its separation while shortening the gradient to the minimum duration. This probes whether cooling can offset compression enough to retain maximum CRF in a faster run.

Narrow the solvent window to reduce gradient steepness and lift the first pair toward baseline resolution while retaining the two-minute gradient. The final peak may elute during the hold, but the stronger separation could recover maximum CRF with a short overall run.

Shift both solvent endpoints upward while preserving the slope that achieved full resolution in injection 6. The stronger final solvent should shorten the last peak’s hold-phase retention; this run tests whether the first pair retains sufficient resolution.

Shift the window upward again at the same successful slope to accelerate the last peak. The first peak should remain retained, while this run checks whether its pair maintains R ≥ 1.5 as the starting organic fraction rises.

Shift the gradient window one more step upward, preserving the slope and temperature that gave full resolution. This should shorten the final peak’s retention while testing whether the early pair remains resolved at the stronger starting solvent.

Raise only the starting organic fraction one grid step to shorten retention while making the gradient shallower. This may improve the critical pair’s separation, but its proximity to the unretained region now needs checking.

Raise temperature one step to shorten the last peak’s retention while testing the available resolution margin of the first pair. Keep the solvent window fixed because the first peak is already approaching the unretained region.

Test the next stronger starting solvent at the cooler temperature that favored the critical pair. This locates the boundary where a shallower gradient’s resolution benefit is overtaken by early-peak compression, while seeking a faster maximum-CRF method.

Return to the resolved starting composition and test the next temperature step above injection 11. This checks the warmest usable setting for the fastest fully resolved method, although the first pair’s small margin makes some loss of resolution likely.

Reduce gradient steepness to try to restore the critical pair’s resolution at 35 C, keeping the starting composition fixed. This tests a warmer, fully resolved alternative, with some expected delay of the final peak during the hold.

Lower the starting organic fraction to move the critical pair farther into the gradient, since flattening the gradient at phi0 = 0.30 barely improved its resolution. This tests whether greater initial retention restores full resolution at 35 C while keeping the run short.

Reduce the endpoint one grid step to make the gradient shallower with the early pair now retained inside it. This should bring its R = 1.42 closer to full resolution, though the final peak will likely elute later than in the fastest maximum-CRF method, injection 11.

Refine around injection 11, the fastest clearly fully resolved method, by lowering the endpoint one step to seek additional resolution margin. Injection 16 sits at the rounded threshold and still flags the first pair, so it is not a robust replacement.

Seek a larger resolution margin by cooling the method from injection 15, where the first pair was limiting. This should provide a short, maximum-CRF alternative with better initial retention than injection 11, which remains the fastest fully resolved method.

Test an intermediate solvent endpoint and temperature near the successful short methods. This may retain full resolution while placing the first peak farther from the unretained region than injection 11, at a modest retention-time cost.

Lower the endpoint one step from injection 19 to increase its narrow resolution margin while keeping the early peaks well retained. This tests a less marginal maximum-CRF alternative; injection 11 remains the fastest fully resolved method found.

Cool injection 17 by one step to increase the critical pair’s resolution margin while retaining a short separation. This refines the neighborhood of the fastest maximum-CRF methods without repeating a tested setting.

Test the remaining intermediate endpoint between injections 9 and 18 at 25 C. It should preserve maximum CRF while balancing early-peak retention, resolution margin, and a shorter final retention time than injection 18.

Extend the local refinement to a shallower gradient at the starting composition that gave the strongest early-pair separation. This should preserve maximum CRF with additional resolution margin, while injection 11 remains the fastest fully resolved option.

Raise temperature one step from injection 23 to shorten the final peak’s retention while using its resolution margin. This completes a local temperature comparison around a successful short method; injection 11 remains the fastest fully resolved method found.

Use the final injection to test whether a stronger endpoint can shorten injection 19 while preserving full resolution with better early-peak retention than injection 11. The first pair may fall just below threshold; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.
